synopsis: You've just moved to Tokyo as an international student. Survive a lost ticket, a late-night konbini run and your first job interview — armed with nothing but your Japanese.

episodes.title: The Lost Ticket
episodes.goal: Get from Shinjuku Station to your new dorm in Kichijoji.
episodes.synopsis: Day 1. Your ticket has vanished somewhere between the airport and the ticket gates. A station attendant is your only hope.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Day 1. You've just arrived in Tokyo. Your new dorm is in Kichijoji — a short train ride away.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: At the crowded ticket gates of Shinjuku Station, you reach into your pocket… Your ticket is gone!

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: あれ？きっぷがない…！
lines.reading: Are? Kippu ga nai…!
lines.translation: Huh? My ticket's gone…!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A station attendant is standing by the gates. Time to get his attention.

choices.text: すみません！
choices.feedback: すみません is the go-to 'excuse me' for getting a stranger's attention — polite and natural.
choices.why: すみません works as 'excuse me', 'sorry' and even 'thanks for the trouble'. Opening with it is the standard, polite way to start any request to a stranger or a member of staff.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: はい！どうしましたか？

choices.text: おい！
choices.feedback: おい is a rough 'hey!' used between close friends — shouting it at staff sounds rude.
choices.why: おい is a blunt 'hey!' used mostly between close friends, or by someone talking down to another person. Toward staff or strangers it sounds rude or angry. Safe alternatives: すみません or あのう….

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: わっ！…は、はい？

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: He jumps. A few commuters turn around to stare.

choices.text: ありがとうございます！
choices.feedback: That's 'thank you' — but he hasn't helped yet! Use すみません to get someone's attention.
choices.why: ありがとうございます thanks someone for help they've given. To open a conversation before any help has happened, Japanese uses すみません. Save ありがとうございます for afterwards (ありがとうございました once the help is finished).

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: え？まだ{何|なに}もしていませんよ。
reaction.reading: E? Mada nani mo shite imasen yo.
reaction.translation: Huh? I haven't done anything yet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He waits for you to explain what happened.

choices.text: きっぷをなくしました。
choices.feedback: なくしました is the polite past of なくす (to lose) — clear, and exactly what happened.
choices.why: なくす = to lose (an object). ～ました is the polite past, and を marks the thing you lost: きっぷをなくしました. Japanese usually drops 'I' and 'my' because the context makes it clear.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: そうですか。{大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}ですよ。
reaction.reading: Sou desu ka. Daijoubu desu yo.
reaction.translation: I see. Don't worry, it's okay.

choices.text: きっぷをください。
choices.feedback: He'll get that you want a ticket, but not that you LOST one — なくしました means 'I lost it'.
choices.why: 〜をください = 'please give me ~'. That's a request, not an explanation. Staff need to know what happened first, so report it in the past tense (なくしました) and then ask.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: きっぷは、あちらで{買|か}えますよ。
reaction.reading: Kippu wa, achira de kaemasu yo.
reaction.translation: You can buy tickets over there.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: …あれ？きっぷをなくしましたか？

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: は、はい…！

choices.text: きっぷはおいしいです。
choices.feedback: おいしい means 'delicious'! To say you lost something, use なくしました.
choices.why: [thing] は [adjective] です describes something, and おいしい means 'delicious'. To report a problem you need a verb: なくしました (lost), わすれました (forgot), こわれました (broke).

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: はは！きっぷは{食|た}べませんよ！

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: …もしかして、なくしましたか？
reaction.translation: …Did you, by any chance, lose it?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: はい…

lines.speaker: tanaka
lines.text: どこから{来|き}ましたか？
lines.reading: Doko kara kimashita ka?
lines.translation: Where did you come from?

choices.text: {成田|なりた}{空港|くうこう}の{駅|えき}から{来|き}ました。
choices.reading: Narita kuukou no eki kara kimashita.
choices.translation: I came from Narita Airport station.
choices.feedback: He meant which station your trip started from — place + から + 来ました answers it perfectly.
choices.why: どこから来ましたか？ = 'Where did you come from?'. At a station that means your departure station. Answer with place + から + 来ました, or more simply: 成田空港駅からです.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: {成田|なりた}からですね。わかりました。
reaction.translation: From Narita, I see. Got it.

choices.text: {私|わたし}の{国|くに}から{来|き}ました！
choices.feedback: Perfect grammar — but he meant which STATION, not which country. Context matters!
choices.why: どこから来ましたか？ is also how people ask a foreigner where they're from, so this mix-up is really common! The situation (a ticket problem at a station) shows he means the station. A clearer way to ask about nationality is お国はどちらですか？

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: はは、{遠|とお}いですね！…でも、どこの{駅|えき}ですか？
reaction.reading: Haha, tooi desu ne! …Demo, doko no eki desu ka?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: あ…{成田|なりた}{空港|くうこう}の{駅|えき}です。
reaction.reading: A… Narita kuukou no eki desu.

choices.text: はい、{来|き}ました。
choices.feedback: どこ asks 'where?' — a yes/no answer doesn't fit. Reply with a place + から.
choices.why: どこ is a question word (where?), so the answer must contain a place. はい／いいえ only answer yes/no questions, which have no question word: 成田から来ましたか？ → はい、来ました.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: ええと…どこの{駅|えき}からですか？
reaction.reading: Eeto… doko no eki kara desu ka?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: あ！{成田|なりた}{空港|くうこう}です！

lines.speaker: tanaka
lines.text: わかりました。では、{新|あたら}しいきっぷを{買|か}ってください。
lines.reading: Wakarimashita. Dewa, atarashii kippu o katte kudasai.
lines.translation: Understood. In that case, please buy a new ticket.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Better find out the price.

choices.text: いくらですか？
choices.feedback: いくら + ですか is the standard polite way to ask a price.
choices.why: いくら = how much, and ですか turns it into a polite question. いくらですか？ works for any price, in shops, stations and restaurants.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: {二百三十円|にひゃくさんじゅうえん}です。

choices.text: いくら？
choices.feedback: A bare いくら？ is fine with friends, but with staff add ですか: いくらですか？
choices.why: Dropping です／ます gives plain (casual) speech. That's fine with friends, but with staff and strangers it can sound curt. Keep です／ます as your default with anyone you don't know.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: …{二百三十円|にひゃくさんじゅうえん}です。

choices.text: どこですか？
choices.feedback: どこ means 'where'. For prices, the question word is いくら (how much).
choices.why: Question words aren't interchangeable: どこ (where), いくら (how much), いつ (when), なに／なん (what), だれ (who). The word before ですか decides what you're asking.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: {券売機|けんばいき}は…そこですよ？
reaction.translation: The ticket machine is… right there?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point at the fare chart instead. He catches on.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: あ、{二百三十円|にひゃくさんじゅうえん}です。

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You pay and get a fresh ticket.

lines.speaker: tanaka
lines.text: {電車|でんしゃ}は{五番線|ごばんせん}です。{改札|かいさつ}はこちらです。
lines.reading: Densha wa go-bansen desu. Kaisatsu wa kochira desu.
lines.translation: Your train is on platform 5. The ticket gate is this way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He said that pretty fast. Which platform was it again?

choices.text: {五番線|ごばんせん}ですね。ありがとうございます！
choices.translation: Platform 5, right? Thank you very much!
choices.feedback: Repeating key info with 〜ですね confirms it politely — and now the thank-you lands at the right moment.
choices.why: Number + 番線 = platform number (五番線 = platform 5). Repeating the information back with 〜ですね ('…, right?') naturally confirms that you heard it correctly. And ありがとうございます fits now, because he has helped.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: はい！{改札|かいさつ}を{通|とお}って、{右|みぎ}です。{気|き}をつけて！
reaction.reading: Hai! Kaisatsu o tootte, migi desu. Ki o tsukete!
reaction.translation: Yes! Through the gate and to the right. Take care!

choices.text: {九番線|きゅうばんせん}ですね。ありがとう！
choices.feedback: He said 五 (go, 5) — not 九 (kyuu, 9). Also, ありがとうございます is politer with staff.
choices.why: ご (5) / きゅう (9) and いち (1) / しち (7) are easy to mishear. Staff often say numbers quickly, so repeating them back gives them a chance to correct you. Also, ありがとう without ございます is casual.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: はい、{気|き}をつけて！

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: He's already turned to help the next passenger. Nobody caught your mistake…

choices.text: すみません、わかりません。もう{一度|いちど}お{願|ねが}いします。
choices.translation: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Once more, please.
choices.feedback: Asking someone to repeat is a real skill — もう一度お願いします is polite and natural.
choices.why: もう一度お願いします ('once more, please') and ゆっくりお願いします ('slowly, please') are survival phrases. Starting with すみません、わかりません softens the request. Asking is always better than guessing.

reaction.speaker: tanaka
reaction.text: ご・ばん・せん。{五番線|ごばんせん}です！

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: {五番線|ごばんせん}！ありがとうございます！

lines.speaker: tanaka
lines.text: {日本語|にほんご}、{上手|じょうず}ですね！
lines.reading: Nihongo, jouzu desu ne!
lines.translation: Your Japanese is really good!

lines.speaker: tanaka
lines.text: これ、どうぞ。{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くのおいしいラーメン{屋|や}です。
lines.reading: Kore, douzo. Eki no chikaku no oishii raamen-ya desu.
lines.translation: Here, take this. It's a great ramen shop near the station.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He sketches a little map on the back of a timetable. Your first night in Tokyo just got delicious.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You find platform 5, squeeze onto the train and watch Tokyo blur past the window.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Forty minutes later you're standing outside your dorm in Kichijoji. Tired — but you made it.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: {電車|でんしゃ}で{着|つ}きました…！
lines.reading: Densha de tsukimashita…!
lines.translation: Made it here by train…!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You hop on a train at platform 9. The doors slide shut behind you…

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: An hour later, you smell salt in the air. Seagulls. This is definitely not Kichijoji.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: ここは…どこですか？
lines.reading: Koko wa… doko desu ka?
lines.translation: Where… am I?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you can move, a student with a tote bag taps your shoulder.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: あの、{大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}ですか？「わかりません」って{言|い}えるの、すごいですね！
lines.reading: Ano, daijoubu desu ka? "Wakarimasen" tte ieru no, sugoi desu ne!
lines.translation: Um, are you okay? Being able to say 'I don't understand' — that's awesome!

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: {私|わたし}も{吉祥寺|きちじょうじ}に{帰|かえ}ります。{一緒|いっしょ}に{行|い}きましょう！
lines.reading: Watashi mo Kichijouji ni kaerimasu. Issho ni ikimashou!
lines.translation: I'm heading back to Kichijoji too. Let's go together!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yuki overheard your 'from my country!' answer and couldn't stop smiling. She walks you all the way to your dorm. Your first friend in Japan.

endings.title: Smooth Commuter
endings.summary: Tanaka-san was so impressed he drew you a map to his favourite ramen shop.
endings.teachingPoint: すみません → explain → いくらですか → confirm with 〜ですね: four moves that solve almost any station problem.

endings.title: Made It!
endings.summary: A few bumps along the way, but you got a new ticket and reached your dorm.
endings.teachingPoint: なくしました (I lost it) and いくらですか (how much?) will save you again and again.

endings.title: Seaside Detour
endings.summary: You mixed up 五 (go, 5) and 九 (kyuu, 9) and rode all the way to the sea.
endings.teachingPoint: Numbers are easy to mishear. Repeat them back (五番線ですね？) or ask: もう一度お願いします.

endings.title: A Friend at the Gate
endings.summary: Your charming 'from my country!' mix-up — and your honest わかりません — caught Yuki's attention. She walked you home.
endings.teachingPoint: Saying わかりません isn't failure. Honest questions start conversations.

phrases.text: すみません、きっぷをなくしました。
phrases.translation: Excuse me, I lost my ticket.
phrases.note: Reporting a problem: すみません + what happened

phrases.text: もう{一度|いちど}お{願|ねが}いします。

grammar.title: 〜をなくしました: reporting what happened
grammar.explanation: [object] を + verb in the ました form describes something that happened. を marks the object, and 'I' and 'my' are usually left out.
grammar.example: さいふをなくしました。

grammar.title: Question words decide the answer
grammar.explanation: どこ (where) needs a place, いくら (how much) a price and いつ (when) a time. Only questions without a question word take はい／いいえ.
grammar.example: どこから来ましたか？ — 成田からです。
grammar.exampleTranslation: Where did you come from? — From Narita.

grammar.title: 〜ですね: checking you understood
grammar.explanation: ね at the end of a sentence asks for agreement ('…, right?'). Repeating key information + ですね is a polite way to confirm it.

quiz.question: A station attendant is standing nearby. What's the most natural way to get his attention?
options: ありがとうございます！
quiz.explanation: すみません is the standard polite way to get someone's attention.

quiz.question: At the station, staff ask どこから来ましたか？ What do they want to know?
quiz.explanation: In a station, どこから means where your journey started, so the station.

quiz.question: How do you ask the price?
quiz.explanation: いくら = how much. どこ = where, いつ = when, なん = what.

survival.title: Which platform?
survival.context: You want to go to Shibuya and ask a station attendant.

steps.speaker: tanaka
steps.text: {渋谷|しぶや}ですか？{山手線|やまのてせん}で、{三番線|さんばんせん}です。
steps.reading: Shibuya desu ka? Yamanote-sen de, san-bansen desu.
steps.translation: Shibuya? Take the Yamanote Line from platform 3.

choices.text: {三番線|さんばんせん}ですね。ありがとうございます。
choices.feedback: You confirmed the platform number. Perfect.
choices.why: Number + 番線 is the platform. Repeating it with ですね lets him correct you if you misheard.

choices.text: {四番線|よんばんせん}ですね。ありがとうございます。
choices.feedback: He said 三 (san, 3), not 四 (yon, 4).
choices.why: さん (3) and よん (4) are both short. Listen carefully and confirm numbers out loud.

choices.text: {渋谷|しぶや}はどこですか？
choices.feedback: He's already answering that. Listen for the platform number.
choices.why: When someone answers your question, show you understood by repeating the key detail instead of asking again.

survival.title: Running late
survival.context: You're waiting on the platform when the attendant walks over.

steps.speaker: tanaka
steps.text: すみません、{次|つぎ}の{電車|でんしゃ}は{十分|じゅっぷん}{遅|おく}れています。
steps.reading: Sumimasen, tsugi no densha wa juppun okurete imasu.
steps.translation: Sorry, the next train is running ten minutes late.

choices.text: わかりました。{十分|じゅっぷん}ですね。
choices.feedback: You acknowledged it and confirmed the delay.
choices.why: 十分 is read じゅっぷん when it means '10 minutes'. わかりました + repeating the detail is the natural response.

choices.text: {十分|じゅうぶん}です！
choices.feedback: じゅうぶん means 'enough'. For ten minutes, say じゅっぷん.
choices.why: 十分 has two readings: じゅっぷん (10 minutes) and じゅうぶん (enough). Here じゅうぶんです sounds like you're telling him to stop talking!

choices.text: はい、{遅|おそ}いです。
choices.feedback: He'll get it, but わかりました is how you acknowledge information.
choices.why: 遅い is an adjective (slow or late). To acknowledge news, use わかりました or そうですか.

survival.title: Not enough balance
survival.context: The gate beeps and won't let you through. You go to the attendant's window.

steps.speaker: tanaka
steps.text: {残高|ざんだか}が{足|た}りませんね。チャージしますか？
steps.reading: Zandaka ga tarimasen ne. Chaaji shimasu ka?
steps.translation: Your balance isn't enough. Would you like to top up?

choices.text: はい、チャージします。
choices.feedback: Exactly. You can't exit without topping up.
choices.why: チャージする = to top up an IC card. Answering with the same verb (チャージします) is natural.

choices.text: いいえ、{大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}です。
choices.feedback: Polite, but you can't get through the gate without topping up!
choices.why: 大丈夫です declines an offer. Here the offer is the only way out, so declining doesn't solve your problem.

choices.text: {残高|ざんだか}をください。
choices.feedback: You can't ask for 'balance'. Say チャージします (I'll top up).
choices.why: 残高 means 'balance (remaining amount)'. To add money, you charge (チャージ) your card.

survival.title: Urgent!
survival.context: You really need the restroom. You find the attendant.

choices.text: すみません、トイレはどこですか？
choices.reading: Sumimasen, toire wa doko desu ka?
choices.translation: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
choices.feedback: Clear and polite.
choices.why: [place] はどこですか？ is the go-to pattern for asking where something is.

choices.text: トイレをなくしました。
choices.feedback: なくしました = I lost it. You didn't lose a toilet!
choices.why: Don't reuse a phrase just because it worked before. Ask for a place with はどこですか.

choices.text: トイレ！
choices.feedback: One word works in an emergency, but the full question is easy and polite.
choices.why: Single words get understood, but すみません + full sentence sounds much more natural to staff.

survival.title: Lost and found
survival.context: You left something on the train and go to the station office.

choices.text: さいふをなくしました。
choices.feedback: You named what you lost. That's exactly what he needs.
choices.why: 何 asks 'what?', so answer with the thing (さいふ = wallet) + をなくしました.

choices.text: はい、なくしました。
choices.feedback: 何 asks 'what?'. Name the item.
choices.why: Questions with a question word (何, どこ, いつ) can't be answered with はい／いいえ.

choices.text: さいふをください。
choices.feedback: ください asks for something. He needs to know what you lost.
choices.why: 〜をください requests an item, but here you have to report something that happened (past tense).

survival.title: West exit
survival.context: You need the WEST exit. You ask the attendant.

steps.speaker: tanaka
steps.text: {東口|ひがしぐち}は{右|みぎ}、{西口|にしぐち}は{左|ひだり}です。
steps.reading: Higashiguchi wa migi, nishiguchi wa hidari desu.
steps.translation: The east exit is on the right, the west exit on the left.

choices.text: {西口|にしぐち}は{左|ひだり}ですね。ありがとうございます。
choices.reading: Nishiguchi wa hidari desu ne. Arigatou gozaimasu.
choices.translation: The west exit is on the left, right? Thank you.
choices.feedback: You picked out the detail you needed and confirmed it.
choices.why: 西 = west, 東 = east, 右 = right, 左 = left. Confirm with ですね.

choices.text: {西口|にしぐち}は{右|みぎ}ですね。ありがとうございます。
choices.reading: Nishiguchi wa migi desu ne. Arigatou gozaimasu.
choices.translation: The west exit is on the right, right? Thank you.
choices.feedback: 右 = right, 左 = left. The west exit is on the left.
choices.why: みぎ (right) and ひだり (left) are easy to swap. Think 'hidari, hand on the left'.

choices.text: {東口|ひがしぐち}ですね。
choices.feedback: You wanted the west exit (西口), not the east (東口).
choices.why: When someone gives you two options, listen for the one you asked about.

episodes.title: Konbini Night
episodes.goal: Buy dinner at the convenience store without panicking.
episodes.synopsis: Day 3, 9 p.m. You're starving, and the konbini clerk speaks in rapid-fire set phrases.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Day 3. It's 9 p.m., you're starving, and the glowing convenience store on the corner is calling your name.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The door chimes as you step inside.

lines.speaker: kenta
lines.text: いらっしゃいませ〜！
lines.reading: Irasshaimase~!
lines.translation: Welcome~!

choices.text: （{軽|かる}く{会釈|えしゃく}する）
choices.feedback: いらっしゃいませ doesn't need a reply — a small nod (or nothing at all) is what locals do.
choices.why: In Japanese shops, いらっしゃいませ is a greeting from staff, not a question, so no answer is expected. Most people say nothing or give a small nod (会釈, a slight bow).

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The clerk — his name tag says KENTA — nods back and returns to stacking rice balls.

choices.text: いらっしゃいませ！
choices.feedback: いらっしゃいませ is what STAFF say to customers — saying it back makes it sound like you work here!
choices.why: いらっしゃいませ is a fixed honorific phrase meaning 'welcome (to our place)', and only the host or staff say it. As a customer you can nod, or say こんにちは to staff you know.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: えっ？…あ、{新|あたら}しいバイトの{方|かた}ですか？
reaction.reading: E? …A, atarashii baito no kata desu ka?
reaction.translation: Huh? …Oh, are you the new part-timer?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: い、いいえ！{客|きゃく}です！

choices.text: はじめまして。どうぞよろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
choices.translation: How do you do. I look forward to our relationship.
choices.feedback: That's a formal self-introduction — lovely at a job interview, but far too much for walking into a shop.
choices.why: はじめまして / どうぞよろしくお願いします introduce you to someone you'll have an ongoing relationship with, such as classmates, coworkers or interviewers. A clerk greeting customers doesn't need one.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: え、あ、はい…よろしくお{願|ねが}いします…？

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You wander the aisles. Sandwiches, ice cream, a whole wall of drinks… but no rice balls anywhere.

choices.text: すみません、おにぎりはどこにありますか？
choices.reading: Sumimasen, onigiri wa doko ni arimasu ka?
choices.translation: Excuse me, where are the rice balls?
choices.feedback: Objects use あります (to exist) — おにぎりはどこにありますか is exactly right.
choices.why: Japanese has two verbs for 'to exist': あります for things (objects, plants, events) and います for people and animals. [thing] はどこにありますか asks where something is.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: おにぎりは、こちらにあります！
reaction.translation: The rice balls are right over here!

choices.text: すみません、おにぎりはどこにいますか？
choices.reading: Sumimasen, onigiri wa doko ni imasu ka?
choices.translation: Excuse me, where are the rice balls (hanging out)?
choices.feedback: います is for living things (people, animals). For objects use あります — otherwise your onigiri sound like they're wandering around!
choices.why: います is only for living things that move by themselves: 猫がいます, 先生がいます. Using it for rice balls turns them into little creatures. Memory trick: あ for 'artifacts', い for 'individuals'.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: あはは！おにぎりは{生|い}きていませんよ。こちらにあります。
reaction.reading: Ahaha! Onigiri wa ikite imasen yo. Kochira ni arimasu.
reaction.translation: Ahaha! The rice balls aren't alive. They're over here.

choices.text: すみません、おにぎりをどこですか？
choices.reading: Sumimasen, onigiri o doko desu ka?
choices.translation: Excuse me, rice balls (object) where is?
choices.feedback: を marks the object of a verb, but there's no action verb here. Use は: おにぎりはどこですか？
choices.why: を marks the object of an action verb (おにぎりを買います). です isn't an action, so it has no object. Mark the topic you're asking about with は: おにぎりはどこですか？

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: おにぎり…を？…あ、おにぎりですね！こちらにあります。
reaction.reading: Onigiri… o? …A, onigiri desu ne! Kochira ni arimasu.
reaction.translation: Rice balls… what? …Oh, rice balls! They're over here.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Onigiri secured. You also grab a karaage bento and head to the register.

lines.speaker: kenta
lines.text: お{弁当|べんとう}、{温|あたた}めますか？
lines.reading: Obentou, atatamemasu ka?
lines.translation: Shall I heat up your bento?

choices.text: はい、お{願|ねが}いします。
choices.feedback: 温めますか？ is an offer — はい、お願いします accepts it politely.
choices.why: 温めますか？ is the polite ます form of 温める (to warm up): 'Shall I heat it?'. Konbini staff ask this for bento. Answer はい、お願いします (yes, please) or 大丈夫です (no, thanks).

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: はい、{少々|しょうしょう}お{待|ま}ちください！

choices.text: はい、{温|あたた}かいです。
choices.feedback: 温かい means 'is warm' — he was OFFERING to heat it (温めますか). Accept with はい、お願いします.
choices.why: 温める is a verb (to heat something) and 温かい is an adjective (warm). The clerk asked about an action, whether to heat it, not about how warm it is now.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: え？…{冷|つめ}たいですよ？

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: He looks at the bento, then at you, then quietly bags it. Unheated.

choices.text: {温|あたた}めません。
choices.feedback: 温めません sounds like YOU refuse to heat it. To decline politely, say 大丈夫です (I'm fine).
choices.why: 温めません is a plain negative: 'I/we won't heat it'. It sounds like a refusal or an announcement. To decline politely, Japanese prefers soft phrases: 大丈夫です, いいです, or 結構です (more formal).

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: あ…はい。そのままですね。
reaction.reading: A… hai. Sono mama desu ne.
reaction.translation: Oh… okay. As it is, then.

lines.speaker: kenta
lines.text: {袋|ふくろ}はご{利用|りよう}ですか？
lines.reading: Fukuro wa goriyou desu ka?
lines.translation: Will you be using a bag?

choices.text: {大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}です。
choices.feedback: 大丈夫です is the softest way to say 'no thanks' in a shop — very natural.
choices.why: 大丈夫です literally means 'I'm all right'. In shops it's the softest way to decline, meaning 'I'm fine without it'. The context makes the meaning clear, so you never have to say いいえ.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: ありがとうございます！

choices.text: はい、ふくろうをください。
choices.feedback: ふくろう (fukurou) is an owl! A bag is ふくろ (fukuro) — vowel length changes the word.
choices.why: Long vowels change meaning: ふくろ (bag) has three short syllables, but ふくろう (owl) ends in a long 'o'. Similar pairs are おばさん / おばあさん (aunt / grandma) and ここ / こうこう (here / high school).

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: ふ、ふくろう…ですか？

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: あはは！{袋|ふくろ}ですね。はい、どうぞ！
reaction.reading: Ahaha! Fukuro desu ne. Hai, douzo!
reaction.translation: Ahaha! You mean a bag. Here you go!

choices.text: はい、{袋|ふくろ}をご{利用|りよう}します。
choices.translation: Yes, I shall honourably use a bag.
choices.feedback: ご利用 is the honorific staff use for YOUR actions — don't use it about yourself. Just say はい、お願いします.
choices.why: ご利用 is honorific: it raises the listener's action, so staff use it for customers (ご利用ですか？). Using honorific forms about yourself sounds self-important. About yourself, say はい、お願いします or 袋をください.

reaction.speaker: kenta
reaction.text: …はい、かしこまりました。

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: As you pay, the door chimes again. It's the student from the room next to yours.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: あ、ゆきさんがいます！
lines.reading: A, Yuki-san ga imasu!
lines.translation: Oh, it's Yuki!

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: あ！{同|おな}じ{寮|りょう}の{人|ひと}だよね？{元気|げんき}？
lines.reading: A! Onaji ryou no hito da yo ne? Genki?
lines.translation: Oh! You live in my dorm, right? How's it going?

choices.text: うん、{元気|げんき}だよ！ゆきちゃんは？
choices.reading: Un, genki da yo! Yuki-chan wa?
choices.translation: Yeah, I'm good! How about you, Yuki?
choices.feedback: She spoke casually (元気？), so matching her with casual だよ sounds friendly and natural.
choices.why: 元気？ is the casual version of 元気ですか？. When a peer speaks to you casually, a casual answer (うん、元気だよ) signals closeness. ～ちゃん is an affectionate suffix often used with friends.

reaction.speaker: yuki
reaction.text: {元気|げんき}{元気|げんき}！{晩|ばん}ごはん？{一緒|いっしょ}に{食|た}べない？
reaction.reading: Genki genki! Bangohan? Issho ni tabenai?
reaction.translation: Doing great! Is that dinner? Want to eat together?

choices.text: はい、{大変|たいへん}{元気|げんき}でございます。
choices.translation: Yes, I am most exceedingly well.
choices.feedback: でございます is ultra-formal (luxury-hotel level). Between students it sounds like a robot butler — match her casual tone.
choices.why: でございます is a super-polite form of です, used by hotel and department-store staff. Japanese has distinct speech levels (casual, polite です／ます, and honorific), and you pick the one that fits the relationship.

reaction.speaker: yuki
reaction.text: あはは！なにそれ、{執事|しつじ}みたい！
reaction.translation: Ahaha! What was that? You sound like a butler!

choices.text: {元気|げんき}ですか？
choices.feedback: Echoing her question back skips your answer — reply first (うん、元気！), then ask back.
choices.why: When someone asks 元気？, answer first (うん、元気！) and then return the question (〇〇は？). Echoing the question without answering leaves the other person hanging.

reaction.speaker: yuki
reaction.text: え？うん、{元気|げんき}だけど…？

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: {温|あたた}かいお{弁当|べんとう}、いいね！{公園|こうえん}で{一緒|いっしょ}に{食|た}べよう！
lines.reading: Atatakai obentou, ii ne! Kouen de issho ni tabeyou!
lines.translation: A warm bento, nice! Let's eat together in the park!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You eat steaming karaage on a park bench while Yuki teaches you her best konbini hacks. Kenta even waves as you leave.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Back in your tiny dorm room, you open a warm bento. Not bad for day three.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: いただきます！
lines.reading: Itadakimasu!
lines.translation: Let's eat! (said before a meal)

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Back in your room, you bite into your karaage bento. It's… refrigerator-cold.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: {冷|つめ}たい…。「{温|あたた}めますか」は{質問|しつもん}だったんだ…
lines.reading: Tsumetai… "Atatamemasu ka" wa shitsumon dattanda…
lines.translation: Cold… So 'atatamemasu ka' was a question…

lines.speaker: kenta
lines.text: また{来|き}てくださいね、ふくろうさん！
lines.reading: Mata kite kudasai ne, Fukurou-san!
lines.translation: Come again soon, Mx. Owl!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The customer who welcomed staff to their own store AND asked for an owl? Kenta tells everyone. By Friday the whole night shift calls you 'Fukurou-san'.

endings.title: Konbini Feast
endings.titleNative: コンビニ・パーティー
endings.summary: Every exchange went smoothly — and Yuki invited you to share dinner in the park.
endings.teachingPoint: Match the register: polite です/ます with staff, casual だよ with friends who speak casually to you.

endings.title: Dinner Secured
endings.summary: You navigated the konbini and brought home a warm dinner.
endings.teachingPoint: 温めますか？ (heat it?) and 袋はご利用ですか？ (bag?) are two questions you'll hear at every konbini.

endings.title: Ice-Cold Karaage
endings.summary: You missed the clerk's offer to heat your bento and ate it fridge-cold.
endings.teachingPoint: 〜ますか？ from staff is often an offer. Accept with はい、お願いします; decline with 大丈夫です.

endings.title: The Owl Legend
endings.summary: Your two best mistakes made you a konbini celebrity: the night shift now calls you 'Fukurou-san'.
endings.teachingPoint: Long vowels matter: ふくろ (bag) vs ふくろう (owl), おばさん (aunt) vs おばあさん (grandma).

phrases.text: はい、お{願|ねが}いします。
phrases.note: Accepting an offer (heating, a bag, a receipt…)
The soft way to decline in shops

phrases.text: おにぎりはどこにありますか？
phrases.reading: Onigiri wa doko ni arimasu ka?

grammar.title: あります vs います
grammar.explanation: あります is for things (objects, plants, events). います is for people and animals.
grammar.example: コンビニがあります。猫がいます。
grammar.exampleTranslation: There's a konbini. There's a cat.

grammar.title: Offers phrased as 〜ますか？
grammar.explanation: Staff often offer services as ます-form questions: 温めますか？ (Shall I heat it?), 袋はご利用ですか？ (Will you use a bag?). Accept with はい、お願いします or decline with 大丈夫です.
grammar.example: お箸はおつけしますか？

grammar.title: Matching speech levels
grammar.explanation: There's casual (だよ), polite (です／ます) and super-polite (でございます). Match the level the other person uses with you: polite with staff, and casual with friends who speak casually to you.
grammar.example: 元気？ — うん、元気だよ！

quiz.question: The clerk says いらっしゃいませ as you walk in. What do most people do?
options: Say いらっしゃいませ back
quiz.explanation: いらっしゃいませ is a staff greeting, and no reply is expected.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly asks where the rice balls are?
options: おにぎりはどこにありますか？
おにぎりはどこにいますか？
おにぎりをどこですか？
quiz.explanation: Things take あります, います is for living things, and を needs an action verb.

quiz.question: The clerk asks 袋はご利用ですか？ and you don't need a bag. What do you say?
quiz.explanation: 大丈夫です declines politely. (ふくろう is an owl!)

survival.title: Receipt?
survival.context: You've just paid at the konbini.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: レシートはご{利用|りよう}ですか？

choices.text: {大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}です。
choices.feedback: The softest way to decline.
choices.why: 大丈夫です politely declines offers in shops.

choices.text: はい、ご{利用|りよう}します。
choices.translation: Yes, I shall honourably use it.
choices.feedback: ご利用 is honorific, for the CUSTOMER's actions. Say はい、お願いします.
choices.why: Honorific forms (ご〜) raise the other person. Using them about yourself sounds self-important.

choices.text: レシートがいます。
choices.feedback: います is for living things, and you'd answer with はい、お願いします anyway.
choices.why: Things use あります, people and animals use います. And an offer needs a yes or no answer.

survival.title: Chopsticks?
survival.context: You're buying a bento at a different konbini.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: お{箸|はし}はおつけしますか？

choices.text: はい、お{願|ねが}いします。
choices.feedback: Simple and polite.
choices.why: おつけしますか？ is a humble offer ('shall I include?'). Accept with はい、お願いします.

choices.text: はい、{箸|はし}をつけます。
choices.feedback: That sounds like YOU will add them. Just accept: はい、お願いします.
choices.why: Echoing the clerk's verb changes who does the action. Accept the offer instead.

choices.text: いいえ、{箸|はし}です。
choices.feedback: That doesn't answer the question. Use はい、お願いします or 大丈夫です.
choices.why: Answer offers with acceptance (お願いします) or a soft decline (大丈夫です).

survival.title: Point card
survival.context: At the register, the clerk asks you something.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: ポイントカードはお{持|も}ちですか？
steps.reading: Pointo kaado wa omochi desu ka?
steps.translation: Do you have a point card?

choices.text: いいえ、{持|も}っていません。
choices.feedback: Clear and polite.
choices.why: 持っています = to have (something on you). Its negative is 持っていません.

choices.text: いいえ、お{持|も}ちではありません。
choices.translation: No, I honourably do not possess one.
choices.feedback: お持ち is honorific, for OTHER people's belongings. For yourself: 持っていません.
choices.why: Honorific お〜 forms talk about others. Use plain polite forms about yourself.

choices.text: はい、ポイントです！
choices.feedback: That doesn't answer whether you have the card.
choices.why: お持ちですか？ asks 'do you have?'. Answer with 持っています or 持っていません.

survival.title: Cash or card?
survival.context: The clerk is ready for you to pay.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: お{支払|しはら}いは{現金|げんきん}ですか、カードですか？
steps.reading: Oshiharai wa genkin desu ka, kaado desu ka?
steps.translation: Will you pay in cash or by card?

choices.text: カードでお{願|ねが}いします。
choices.feedback: You picked one option with で (by means of).
choices.why: 〜で marks the method: カードで, 現金で. Add お願いします to make it polite.

choices.text: はい、そうです。
choices.feedback: It's an either/or question, so pick one: カードで or 現金で.
choices.why: A ですか、〜ですか question asks you to choose, so はい doesn't answer it.

choices.text: カードをなくしました。
choices.feedback: You just told him you lost your card!
choices.why: Make sure the phrase matches the situation. なくしました reports a lost item.

survival.title: Hot or cold?
survival.context: You ask for tea at the counter of a konbini café corner.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: {温|あたた}かいお{茶|ちゃ}と{冷|つめ}たいお{茶|ちゃ}、どちらにしますか？
steps.reading: Atatakai ocha to tsumetai ocha, dochira ni shimasu ka?
steps.translation: Hot tea or cold tea, which would you like?

choices.text: {温|あたた}かいのをお{願|ねが}いします。
choices.feedback: Adjective + の = 'the hot one'. Natural.
choices.why: どちら asks 'which one?'. Adjective + の turns it into 'the ~ one'.

choices.text: はい、お{願|ねが}いします。
choices.feedback: どちら asks 'which one?', so はい doesn't choose.
choices.why: Listen for どちら／どっち. It means you have to pick an option.

choices.text: {温|あたた}めません。
choices.feedback: Nobody asked you to heat anything!
choices.why: 温かい (hot, adjective) ≠ 温める (to heat, verb).

survival.title: Karaoke invite
survival.context: Yuki catches you outside the konbini.

steps.speaker: yuki
steps.text: {明日|あした}、{一緒|いっしょ}にカラオケ{行|い}かない？
steps.translation: Want to go to karaoke together tomorrow?

choices.text: いいね！{行|い}こう！
choices.feedback: Casual invitation → casual, enthusiastic answer.
choices.why: 〜ない？ is a casual invitation. 行こう (let's go) is the casual volitional form.

choices.text: はい、{参|まい}ります。
choices.feedback: 参ります is humble keigo, far too formal for a friend.
choices.why: Humble verbs (参る, いたす, おる) are for superiors and customers, not for friends.

choices.text: いいえ、{行|い}きません！
choices.feedback: Clear, but very blunt. A softer no: ごめん、明日はちょっと…
choices.why: Japanese usually softens refusals. ちょっと… ('it's a bit…') does the job.

episodes.title: The Café Interview
episodes.goal: Land your first part-time job at Café Komorebi.
episodes.synopsis: Day 6. Your savings are melting. Yuki got you an interview — now switch from casual chat with her to keigo with the manager.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Day 6. Your savings are melting faster than konbini ice cream. Time for a part-time job.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yuki works at Café Komorebi and set up an interview for you. You arrive ten minutes early.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: {来|き}たね！{店長|てんちょう}、もうすぐ{来|く}るよ。{緊張|きんちょう}してる？
lines.reading: Kita ne! Tenchou, mou sugu kuru yo. Kinchou shiteru?
lines.translation: You made it! The manager'll be here soon. Nervous?

choices.text: ちょっとね。でも{頑張|がんば}る！
choices.translation: A little. But I'll do my best!
choices.feedback: Casual ちょっとね + 頑張る matches Yuki's friendly tone perfectly.
choices.why: Casual speech drops です／ます, so 頑張る instead of 頑張ります. ちょっとね ('a little, yeah') is a soft casual reply. Matching your friend's register keeps the conversation warm.

reaction.speaker: yuki
reaction.text: その{調子|ちょうし}！{店長|てんちょう}は{優|やさ}しいから{大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}だよ。
reaction.reading: Sono choushi! Tenchou wa yasashii kara daijoubu da yo.
reaction.translation: That's the spirit! The manager's kind, so you'll be fine.

choices.text: はい、{少々|しょうしょう}{緊張|きんちょう}しております。
choices.translation: Yes, I am feeling somewhat nervous. (humble)
choices.feedback: おります is humble keigo — save it for the manager. With a friend it sounds stiff and distant.
choices.why: 〜ております is humble keigo (謙譲語): you lower yourself to show respect to a superior or a customer. Using it with a friend creates distance, as if you were strangers.

reaction.speaker: yuki
reaction.text: あはは、{面接|めんせつ}はまだだよ！{私|わたし}にはふつうでいいよ。
reaction.reading: Ahaha, mensetsu wa mada da yo! Watashi ni wa futsuu de ii yo.
reaction.translation: Haha, the interview hasn't started yet! Just talk normally with me.

choices.text: {緊張|きんちょう}？してないよ。{余裕|よゆう}{余裕|よゆう}。
choices.feedback: Natural casual Japanese, just a bit cocky — and you're still in casual mode right before a formal talk.
choices.why: 余裕 means 'room to spare', and 余裕余裕 is slang for 'easy-peasy'. It's grammatically fine, but it sounds overconfident, and you'll have to switch gears for the manager in a minute.

reaction.speaker: yuki
reaction.text: ほんと？{店長|てんちょう}の{前|まえ}では{敬語|けいご}だよ？
reaction.reading: Honto? Tenchou no mae de wa keigo da yo?
reaction.translation: Really? You know it's keigo in front of the manager, right?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A woman in a linen apron walks over. Yuki straightens up and slips back behind the counter.

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: はじめまして。{店長|てんちょう}の{佐藤|さとう}です。どうぞ、おかけください。
lines.reading: Hajimemashite. Tenchou no Satou desu. Douzo, okake kudasai.
lines.translation: Nice to meet you. I'm Sato, the manager. Please, have a seat.

choices.text: はじめまして。{本日|ほんじつ}はよろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
choices.reading: Hajimemashite. Honjitsu wa yoroshiku onegai itashimasu.
choices.translation: Nice to meet you. Thank you for your time today.
choices.feedback: 本日 + よろしくお願いいたします is textbook interview keigo — polite without overdoing it.
choices.why: Interviews use set phrases: はじめまして → (name)と申します → 本日はよろしくお願いいたします. 本日 is the formal word for 'today', and いたします is the humble form of します.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: はい、よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。

choices.text: はじめまして！よろしく！
choices.translation: Nice to meet ya! Hey there!
choices.feedback: A bare よろしく is casual — you carried Yuki's tone into the interview. Use よろしくお願いいたします.
choices.why: よろしく on its own is casual. The ladder goes よろしく → よろしくお願いします → よろしくお願いいたします. In formal settings like interviews, use the longest form.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: …よ、よろしく。

choices.text: はじめまして、{佐藤|さとう}{店長|てんちょう}さん。よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
choices.translation: Nice to meet you, Mrs. Manager Sato. Pleased to meet you.
choices.feedback: 店長 is already a title, so 佐藤店長さん doubles the honorific. 佐藤店長 on its own is right.
choices.why: Job titles like 店長, 部長 and 先生 already work as honorifics, so attach them straight to the name: 佐藤店長. Adding さん on top (佐藤店長さん) doubles the honorific. The same goes for 田中先生.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: ふふ、「{佐藤|さとう}」でいいですよ。

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: では、どうしてうちで{働|はたら}きたいんですか？
lines.reading: Dewa, doushite uchi de hatarakitai n desu ka?
lines.translation: So, why do you want to work here?

choices.text: {日本語|にほんご}を{使|つか}って、お{客|きゃく}さんと{話|はな}したいからです。
choices.reading: Nihongo o tsukatte, okyakusan to hanashitai kara desu.
choices.translation: Because I want to use my Japanese and talk with customers.
choices.feedback: A reason about growth and customers — exactly what interviewers hope to hear, in clean です form.
choices.why: Interviewers want motivation connected to the job: 〜たいからです ('because I want to ~'). Mentioning learning, customers or the shop itself sounds sincere.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: いいですね。うちはお{客|きゃく}さんとよく{話|はな}しますよ。
reaction.reading: Ii desu ne. Uchi wa okyakusan to yoku hanashimasu yo.
reaction.translation: Great. We chat with customers a lot here.

choices.text: {時給|じきゅう}がいいからです。
choices.translation: Because the hourly pay is good.
choices.feedback: Grammatically perfect and honest — but leading with money sounds blunt in a Japanese interview.
choices.why: Pay matters, but in Japanese interviews it usually comes up after you've shown interest in the work itself. Answering if you're asked is fine. Just don't lead with it.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: …{正直|しょうじき}ですね。{時給|じきゅう}は{千二百円|せんにひゃくえん}です。
reaction.reading: …Shoujiki desu ne. Jikyuu wa sen nihyaku en desu.
reaction.translation: …You're honest. The hourly wage is 1,200 yen.

choices.text: コーヒーが{大好|だいす}きだからっす！
choices.feedback: 〜っす is sporty slang for です — friendly between coworkers, but too casual for a first interview.
choices.why: 〜っす is a contraction of です used by young people and in sports clubs. It's friendly with coworkers and seniors you're close to, but too casual for a first meeting with a manager.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: 「っす」…ふふ。コーヒー、{好|す}きなんですね。
reaction.reading: "Ssu"… fufu. Koohii, suki nan desu ne.
reaction.translation: 'Ssu'… heh. So you love coffee, huh.

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: いつから{働|はたら}けますか？
lines.reading: Itsu kara hatarakemasu ka?
lines.translation: When can you start working?

choices.text: {来週|らいしゅう}の{月曜日|げつようび}から{働|はたら}けます。
choices.translation: I can start from next Monday.
choices.feedback: いつから asks 'from when' — a start date + 働けます (can work) answers it precisely.
choices.why: いつから = 'from when?'. 働けます ('can work') is the polite potential form (働く → 働ける → 働けます). Answering with a specific date (来週の月曜日から) is clear and helpful.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: {来週|らいしゅう}ですね。{助|たす}かります。

choices.text: {毎日|まいにち}{働|はたら}けます！
choices.feedback: Enthusiastic! But she asked いつから (from WHEN), not how often. Listen for the question word.
choices.why: The question word decides the answer. いつから (from when?) needs a start date, while 週に何日 (how many days a week?) needs a frequency. 毎日 answers the second question, not the first.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: {毎日|まいにち}…？ええと、{始|はじ}められるのはいつですか？
reaction.reading: Mainichi…? Eeto, hajimerareru no wa itsu desu ka?
reaction.translation: Every day…? Um, when can you START?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: あ、{来週|らいしゅう}からです！

choices.text: {来週|らいしゅう}から{働|はたら}きました。
choices.feedback: 働きました is past tense — 'I worked from next week' is time travel! Use 働けます (can work).
choices.why: 働きました is past tense, but 来週 is in the future, so the two clash. For the future use the ます form (働きます) or the potential form (働けます).

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: …{未来|みらい}から{来|き}たんですか？

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: い、いえ！{来週|らいしゅう}から{働|はたら}けます！
reaction.translation: N-no! I can start next week!

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: {最後|さいご}に、{何|なに}か{質問|しつもん}はありますか？
lines.reading: Saigo ni, nanika shitsumon wa arimasu ka?
lines.translation: Finally, do you have any questions?

choices.text: はい。{新|あたら}しいスタッフの{研修|けんしゅう}はありますか？
choices.reading: Hai. Atarashii sutaffu no kenshuu wa arimasu ka?
choices.translation: Yes. Is there training for new staff?
choices.feedback: Asking about training shows you're serious about doing the job well — a great closing question.
choices.why: Ending an interview with a question shows interest, and the best ones are about the work: 研修はありますか, どんな仕事から始めますか. 〜はありますか ('is there ~?') is an easy pattern.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: はい、{最初|さいしょ}の{一週間|いっしゅうかん}は{研修|けんしゅう}です。
reaction.reading: Hai, saisho no isshuukan wa kenshuu desu.
reaction.translation: Yes, the first week is training.

choices.text: {特|とく}にありません。
choices.feedback: Polite and acceptable, but it misses a chance to show interest. Prepare one question in advance.
choices.why: 特にありません is polite and acceptable. But 何か質問はありますか is a chance to show motivation, so it's common advice to prepare one question in advance.

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: そうですか。わかりました。

choices.text: まかないはありますか？
choices.feedback: まかない (staff meals) is a real perk people ask about — natural wording, but a bold opening question!
choices.why: まかない (staff meals) is a real perk at Japanese restaurants and cafés, and people do ask about it, usually once they're hired. As your only question in an interview, it can sound like you mainly want the food!

reaction.speaker: sato
reaction.text: ありますよ。{今日|きょう}のおすすめはチーズケーキです。
reaction.reading: Arimasu yo. Kyou no osusume wa chiizukeeki desu.
reaction.translation: There are. Today's special is cheesecake.

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: {本日|ほんじつ}はありがとうございました。{敬語|けいご}もとても{上手|じょうず}ですね。
lines.reading: Honjitsu wa arigatou gozaimashita. Keigo mo totemo jouzu desu ne.
lines.translation: Thank you for today. Your keigo is excellent, too.

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: ぜひ、{来週|らいしゅう}からよろしくお{願|ねが}いします！
lines.reading: Zehi, raishuu kara yoroshiku onegaishimasu!
lines.translation: We'd love to have you — see you next week!

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: やったね！{一緒|いっしょ}に{働|はたら}けるね！
lines.reading: Yatta ne! Issho ni hatarakeru ne!
lines.translation: You did it! We get to work together!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Two days later, your phone buzzes. It's Café Komorebi.

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: もしもし、{佐藤|さとう}です。ぜひ{来週|らいしゅう}から{働|はたら}いてください！
lines.reading: Moshimoshi, Satou desu. Zehi raishuu kara hataraite kudasai!
lines.translation: Hello, it's Sato. We'd love you to start next week!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Manager Sato thanks you politely… a little too politely. You know what that means.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.text: {大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}！{今日|きょう}から{私|わたし}が{敬語|けいご}の{先生|せんせい}ね。{頑張|がんば}ろう！
lines.reading: Daijoubu! Kyou kara watashi ga keigo no sensei ne. Ganbarou!
lines.translation: It's okay! From today I'm your keigo teacher. Let's do our best!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Over strawberry parfaits, Yuki drills you on です, ます and いたします. Next interview, you'll be ready.

lines.speaker: sato
lines.text: {実|じつ}は{私|わたし}もコーヒーが{大好|だいす}きで…まかないで{新|あたら}しい{豆|まめ}を{試|ため}しませんか？
lines.reading: Jitsu wa watashi mo koohii ga daisuki de… makanai de atarashii mame o tameshimasen ka?
lines.translation: Actually, I love coffee too… Want to try our new beans over a staff meal?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your slightly-too-casual passion struck a chord. Sato hires you as a barista trainee, and you spend the afternoon taste-testing beans.

endings.title: Hired on the Spot
endings.summary: Manager Sato hired you on the spot — and you'll be working shifts with Yuki.
endings.teachingPoint: Switching registers is the real skill: casual with Yuki, keigo (いたします, 本日) with the manager.

endings.title: The Callback
endings.summary: A couple of wobbles, but your effort showed — the café called two days later to offer you the job.
endings.teachingPoint: In interviews, listen for the question word (いつ, どうして, 何) and answer exactly that.

endings.title: Keigo Bootcamp
endings.summary: The interview didn't land — but Yuki turned it into a parfait-fuelled keigo bootcamp.
endings.teachingPoint: Casual (だよ), polite (です/ます) and humble (いたします/おります) are three different gears. Interviews need the top two.

endings.title: Coffee Comrades
endings.summary: Your casual love of coffee (and your bold staff-meal question) turned a stiff interview into a tasting session.
endings.teachingPoint: っす and まかない aren't textbook interview Japanese — but genuine enthusiasm opens doors. Learn the rules, then learn when to bend them.

phrases.text: {本日|ほんじつ}はよろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
phrases.translation: Thank you for your time today.

phrases.text: {来週|らいしゅう}の{月曜日|げつようび}から{働|はたら}けます。
phrases.note: いつから → a start date

phrases.text: {研修|けんしゅう}はありますか？
ちょっとね。でも{頑張|がんば}る！
phrases.translation: A little. But I'll do my best!

grammar.title: Three registers
grammar.explanation: Casual (頑張る), polite (頑張ります) and humble keigo (いたします／おります／申します). Use casual with friends, and humble keigo about yourself in interviews.
grammar.example: よろしく → よろしくお願いします → よろしくお願いいたします

grammar.title: Potential form: 'can do'
grammar.explanation: 働く → 働ける (can work) → 働けます (polite). Use it to say what you're able to do.

grammar.title: Titles work as honorifics
grammar.explanation: 店長, 部長 and 先生 already show respect. Attach them straight to the name (佐藤店長, 田中先生) without an extra さん.
grammar.example: 佐藤店長、よろしくお願いいたします。
grammar.exampleTranslation: Manager Sato, pleased to work with you.

quiz.question: Your friend asks you casually: 緊張してる？ Which reply matches her register?
options: ちょっとね。でも頑張る！
はい、少々緊張しております。
緊張いたしております。
quiz.explanation: A casual question gets a casual answer. おります is humble keigo, for superiors.

quiz.question: The manager asks いつから働けますか？ What is she asking?
quiz.explanation: いつから = from when, so she wants your start date.

quiz.question: Which is the correct way to address the manager?
quiz.explanation: 店長 is a title that already works as an honorific, so no extra さん.

survival.title: First day
survival.context: It's your first shift at Café Komorebi.

steps.speaker: sato
steps.text: {今日|きょう}からよろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
steps.translation: Glad to have you, starting today.

choices.text: よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします！
choices.translation: I look forward to working with you!
choices.feedback: The humble form fits perfectly with your manager.
choices.why: お願いいたします is the humble version, a step more formal than お願いします.

choices.text: よろしく！
choices.feedback: Too casual for your manager.
choices.why: Bare よろしく is for friends. With a boss, use the full phrase.

choices.text: お{疲|つか}れさまでした。
choices.feedback: お疲れさまでした is said at the END of work, not when you arrive.
choices.why: Workplace greetings depend on timing: おはようございます (arriving) and お疲れさまでした (leaving).

survival.title: End of shift
survival.context: Your shift is over and you're heading home.

steps.speaker: sato
steps.text: お{疲|つか}れさまでした。
steps.translation: Thanks for your hard work today.

choices.text: お{疲|つか}れさまでした。お{先|さき}に{失礼|しつれい}します。
choices.reading: Otsukaresama deshita. Osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.
choices.translation: Thanks for your hard work. Excuse me for leaving first.
choices.feedback: Textbook workplace etiquette.
choices.why: お先に失礼します ('excuse me for leaving before you') is what you say when you leave before others.

choices.text: さようなら！
choices.feedback: さようなら sounds like a long goodbye. At work, people say お先に失礼します.
choices.why: さようなら is for goodbyes that might be long, or for school. Workplaces use fixed phrases.

choices.text: はい、{疲|つか}れました。
choices.feedback: Honest! But お疲れさまでした is a greeting, not a question about how you feel.
choices.why: お疲れさま acknowledges effort. Answer by returning it, not by describing how tired you are.

survival.title: Your first customer
survival.context: Kenta from the konbini walks in as a customer.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: すみません、ラテをひとつください。

choices.text: かしこまりました。{少々|しょうしょう}お{待|ま}ちください。
choices.feedback: Perfect customer-service Japanese.
choices.why: かしこまりました is a humble 'understood' used with customers. 少々お待ちください = 'one moment, please'.

choices.text: わかった！ちょっと{待|ま}って。
choices.feedback: Friendly, but too casual for a customer, even if you know him.
choices.why: At work you use customer-service keigo with everyone being served.

choices.text: ラテをください。
choices.feedback: You just repeated his order back as your own request!
choices.why: Acknowledge the order with かしこまりました instead of echoing it.

survival.title: Weekend shift
survival.context: Manager Sato is planning next week's schedule.

steps.speaker: sato
steps.text: {土曜日|どようび}は{働|はたら}けますか？

choices.text: すみません、{土曜日|どようび}はちょっと…
choices.feedback: Softly declining with ちょっと… is very natural Japanese.
choices.why: Japanese often declines indirectly: すみません + [day] はちょっと… The listener understands it's a no.

choices.text: {働|はたら}けません！
choices.feedback: Clear, but abrupt. Add すみません and soften it with ちょっと….
choices.why: A direct 'can't' sounds harsh. Apologize first and leave the sentence soft.

choices.text: {土曜日|どようび}に{働|はたら}きました。
choices.feedback: That's past tense: 'I worked on Saturday.'
choices.why: Answer 働けますか？ with 働けます／働けません (can / can't), not with the past tense.

survival.title: Ask a coworker
survival.context: Yuki checks on you during your shift.

steps.speaker: yuki
steps.text: {何|なに}かわからないことある？

choices.text: うん、カップはどこに{置|お}けばいい？
choices.reading: Un, kappu wa doko ni okeba ii?
choices.translation: Yeah, where should I put the cups?
choices.feedback: Casual and specific. Perfect with a friendly coworker.
choices.why: 〜ばいい？ asks 'what should I do?'. Matching Yuki's casual tone keeps it natural.

choices.text: はい、ございます。
choices.feedback: Far too formal for Yuki, and you didn't say what you need.
choices.why: ございます is very formal. With a friendly coworker, answer casually and be specific.

choices.text: {全部|ぜんぶ}わからない！
choices.feedback: Honest! But a specific question gets you better help.
choices.why: Asking about one concrete thing (どこ, どうやって) makes it easier for people to help.

survival.title: Wrong drink
survival.context: You brought a customer the wrong drink.

steps.speaker: kenta
steps.text: あの、これ、ラテじゃないですよ。
steps.reading: Ano, kore, rate ja nai desu yo.

choices.text: {申|もう}し{訳|わけ}ございません。すぐにお{持|も}ちします。
choices.reading: Moushiwake gozaimasen. Sugu ni omochi shimasu.
choices.translation: I'm terribly sorry. I'll bring it right away.
choices.feedback: A formal apology plus a fix. Excellent.
choices.why: 申し訳ございません is the most formal apology, used with customers. お持ちします is the humble 'I'll bring it'.

choices.text: ごめん！
choices.feedback: ごめん is casual. With customers, use 申し訳ございません.
choices.why: Apologies have levels too: ごめん (casual) → すみません (polite) → 申し訳ございません (formal).

choices.text: ラテですよ。
choices.feedback: Arguing with the customer! Apologize and fix it.
choices.why: In customer service, apologize first and then solve the problem.
